item.title: Rod 002: 6'6" 2pc Light Spinning (French Broad)
item.description:
A two-piece split-cane spinning rod for winter fishing on the French Broad around Hap Simpson Park in Brevard, late November through December. The joint is a spliced (scarf) joint, with a ferrule as the fallback, and both sections are milled on the standard Morgan Hand Mill bed. This is my first spinning rod, so the page also covers the spinning basics a fly-rod builder doesn’t already know: power classes, the reel seat, guides, the reel, and lures.

The spec in one line: 6'6", two piece (splice or 12/64 ferrule), hex, light power / moderate-fast action, 4–6 lb line, lures 1/16–1/4 oz (designed around 1/8 oz), sliding-ring cork grip, a 1000-size reel.

Status: design only. The taper below hasn’t been cut yet. It’s been checked against the library’s spinning rods in caneDNA (see Taper).

The water: French Broad at Hap Simpson, Nov–Dec

  • Where: Hap Simpson Park is a City of Brevard river access with a boat ramp and picnic tables, at about mile 21.5 of the French Broad Paddle Trail. It’s the take-out for the flat, calm ~10-mile float down from Island Ford. The Pisgah Forest access is about 5 miles downstream.
  • What it’s like: The mainstem here is slow, sandy, deep-bend water, not freestone pocket water. In winter, fish hold in the deep slow pools, on the outside bends, and around woody cover. Expect holdover stocked trout and resident browns, plus smallmouth, redbreast sunfish and rock bass, all sluggish in cold water.
  • Regulations (verify before fishing): A third-party county guide lists the mainstem from the West/North Fork junction down to the US 276 bridge as Hatchery Supported trout water. That reach should include Hap Simpson, but I haven’t confirmed it against the NCWRC rule text. Under Hatchery Supported rules: 7 trout/day, no minimum length, and no bait or lure restrictions. You need an NC fishing license plus the trout privilege on designated public mountain trout waters.
  • Best fishing nearby in this window: The fresh fish are in the Delayed Harvest waters. These are the East Fork French Broad (NCWRC scheduled its fall 2026 stocking for Nov 10 after warm water cancelled October) and DuPont’s Little River. DH runs catch-and-release, artificial lures with one single hook only. Build the tackle box around single-hook lures and one kit covers both waters (see Tackle).
  • Stocking caveat: Bobby N. Setzer hatchery, right up the Davidson, closed in late 2025 for renovation, so NCWRC now stocks from Armstrong. Check the NCWRC stocking schedule instead of assuming past patterns.
  • Flows: USGS 03443000, French Broad at Blantyre is the closest mainstem gage below Brevard.

The Brevard / DuPont / Highlands dossier has the rest of the region: shops, the DH calendar, and Helene access notes.

Power class: ultralight vs. light

Spinning rods are rated by power (how much force it takes to bend the rod; roughly, the line and lure weights it handles) and action (where it bends: fast = mostly the tip, moderate = into the middle). This is the spinning equivalent of a fly rod’s line weight.

Class Line Lures Good for Here
Ultralight (UL) 2–4 lb 1/32–1/8 oz small creeks, small fish, short casts Fits the East Fork and creeks. Underpowered for the mainstem’s width, current, and the odd big brown or smallmouth.
Light (L) 4–6 lb 1/16–1/4 oz small rivers, stocked trout, bass Pick this. It casts across the mainstem pools, handles a 1/4 oz spoon or jerkbait, and is still fun on a 10" stocker.
Medium-light (ML) 6–8 lb 1/8–3/8 oz bigger rivers, bass-first fishing Overgunned for winter’s small, slow lures.

Light wins because this rod has to cover both the wide, slow mainstem and the small DH runs, and winter lures are small (1/16–1/8 oz) but sometimes need distance. A bamboo light rod still casts 1/16 oz well, because a cane rod’s own mass helps load it. Thomas & Thomas labeled their classic 5'6" spinner “ultralight,” and a builder who measured one rated it light-to-ultralight in the hand. That’s the feel I’m after here.

Rod spec

key value
geometry hex (6)
rod length 6 ft 6 in (78")
pieces 2, joint at 39" (spliced, or a 12/64 ferrule)
power / action light / moderate-fast
line 4–6 lb mono
lure weight 1/16–1/4 oz (design point 1/8 oz)
tip 0.080" → tiptop tube 6/64
butt (grip) 0.279–0.281"

strip length ~50" per section (incl. splice overlap and cut-offs)

Two pieces: splice or ferrule

The rod is two 39" sections, and the joint is chosen after glue-up: a spliced (scarf) joint or a 12/64 ferrule. Both sections fit the standard Morgan bed, so there’s no extension bed, no 89" strips, and no long heat-treating oven. The class routine (5–6’ culm sections, normal oven) applies as-is.

Mill both sections long through the joint. The tip section runs to about 44" from the tip, and the butt section starts at about 34". That covers half a 4.5" splice on each side of 39", plus cut-offs. Then pick the joint:

  • Splice (preferred). Cut matching 4.5" scarf bevels (on the adjustable scarf jig, set to 1:23.3) on opposite faces, across the flats, from 36.75" to 41.25". 4.5" is about 23 times the 0.193" dimension. Joined, the two bevels restore the full cross-section, so the rod bends like a one-piece and adds no weight. Whip each feather end with a few turns of thread so it can’t lift or split. At the river, lay the bevels together, line up the guides, and wrap the joint tightly with tape (cloth friction tape or self-amalgamating tape).
  • Ferrule (fallback). Trim both sections square at 39" and fit a 12/64 ferrule. The 0.193" flats there are 12.4/64, the same fit as Rod 001’s 12/64 at 0.193". It’s convenient, but on a light spinner the ferrule outweighs the lure: a 12/64 is roughly 0.2 oz (my estimate) against a 1/8 oz lure.

Other notes:

  • Culms and nodes: a 3×3 stagger per section, as in the class build. Keep nodes out of the scarf (36–42"), the top 6" (tiptop), and the reel-ring area.
  • Guides near the joint: put one guide just outside each end of the splice. They double as alignment marks when you tape up.

Taper

No published taper matched the spec, so I designed this one from published bamboo spinning tapers on bamboorodmaking.com:

  • Richard Tyree’s 6’ (lures to 1/4 oz): the closest match, tip 0.079
  • the T&T Classic 5'6" (2–4 lb, to 1/4 oz): tip 0.072
  • Paul H. Young’s 6'4" Spin-Caster: tip 0.096, a heavier tip

The starting point scaled Tyree’s rod to 78" with a nearly straight taper (~0.014–0.016" per 5" station). A tip at 0.080 follows Ian Kearney’s advice that a light open-face rod “needs to come down to closer to .075.” I then ran the taper through caneDNA, my RodDNA-style taper engine, and stiffened it +4% from 10" to 60", with the tip left as-is. That’s the “variant D” in the table below.

caneDNA results

caneDNA uses RodDNA’s casting-load model. I compared this taper against the 16 bamboo spinning rods in its library, including “Spin Rod 6’ 1 pc.”, which is essentially Tyree’s 6’. For the lures, each lure was modeled as a weight at the tip with a 4× impact factor. Stress is averaged from 10" to the grip; lower stress means a stiffer rod.

Taper Stress @ 1/16 oz @ 1/8 oz @ 1/4 oz Recovery (RodDNA load)
First draft (straight Tyree scale-up) 54k 67k 92k 1.87 Hz
Variant D (this taper) 51k 63k 87k 2.00 Hz
Tyree 6’ 1pc (reference) 52k 65k 91k 2.42 Hz
  • Stress level: per lure weight, the rod loads like Tyree’s proven 6’. It sits between the ultralight T&T (higher stress) and the 6–10 lb 7' spinners (lower), which fits the light rating.
  • Recovery: the first draft was the slowest-recovering rod of any 6’+ spinner in the library. Scaling Tyree’s 2.42 Hz to 78" predicts about 2.06, and variant D recovers at 2.00. So D is Tyree’s rod at 6'6".
  • Shape: stress rises toward the butt with light lures, because the cane’s own weight dominates. It flattens at 1/4 oz.
  • Ferrule: a ~0.2 oz 12/64 ferrule at 39" raises butt stress 6–10% between 45" and 60". That’s within the variation from one culm to the next, so the taper doesn’t change. With RodDNA’s own heavier default ferrule weight (0.53 oz) it’s about +30%.
  • Caveats: the frequencies assume a cane stiffness (E) of 2.4 million psi, so compare them between rods rather than as absolutes. This isn’t Hexrod; Hexrod only models fly lines.

Morgan Hand Mill settings

Oversize columns follow the class sheet: rough +0.070, Hand Mill +0.030, finish +0.003 (all per strip, i.e. added to the half dimension). The MHM Setting is the bed rise from the thickest station in each section, the same convention and station layout as Rod 001. Each section’s thin end sits at #12 with the extension at #13. The largest change between adjacent stations is 0.008", well under the bed’s 0.020" limit. caneDNA estimates hold-down hole E for the tip and hole D for the butt.

Handle and reel seat

The big difference from a fly rod is that the reel sits partway up the handle, not at the butt, and it hangs below the rod on a stem. Your casting hand wraps the seat with the reel stem between two fingers. The rear grip runs back along your forearm, and your index finger reaches the spool to feather the line. There’s no line hand: the reel does all the line handling.

Option A (recommended): full cork with sliding rings

The classic bamboo spinning handle (T&T, Paul Young, and the Montague-derived 6’ on bamboorodmaking all use it). It’s just a fly-rod cork grip with no seat hardware. The reel foot sits on the cork and two metal rings slide over its ends.

---------+ | | | | | | |
+-+------------+------+----+---+----+------+------------+---+
winding | | stem
check .--+---+--.
| reel |

|<-------------------------- 12″ cork ------------------------>|
|<------- ~3.5″ ---------->|<------------ ~8.5″ --------------->|
66″ from tip reel-foot center 78″ butt
  • 12" Portuguese cork (78" − 12" = cork starts at 66"). Shape it as one long cigar or a straight full-wells with a slight swell under the reel.
  • Rings: 2 nickel-silver or aluminum sliding rings sized to the cork’s diameter at the reel position, about 7/8–1". Lap the reel foot on the cork first; the rings should press it down snugly, not just touch.
  • Reel position: about 8.5" from the butt end to the center of the reel foot, then fine-tune by balance and forearm length. Hold it the way you’d fish it: the butt end should just reach the inside of your forearm.
  • Tradeoff: the lightest, cleanest, and most period-correct option, but rings can creep when it’s cold and wet. The fix is a strip of electrical tape under the foot or a slight taper in the cork so the rings jam.

Option B: skeleton seat (modern, locks solid)

A graphite skeleton seat (Fuji and ALPS make spinning versions in 16–18 mm) with split fore and rear grips. It’s mounted on a built-up arbor over the hex (masking tape or cork rings shaped round, epoxied).

| | stem

  • Fixed hood on one end, threaded hood plus lock nut on the other. Either direction works. Pick whichever puts the threads where your fingers don’t sit.
  • Tradeoff: the reel never moves, but you’ll have to make an arbor and it looks modern on cane.

Fly vs. spin at a glance

Fly rod Spinning rod
Reel position at the butt, below the grip 8–9" up from the butt, mid-handle
Reel orientation hangs below hangs below on a stem
What carries the cast the line’s weight the lure’s weight
Line control line hand strips line index finger on the spool, then turn the handle
Guides small snakes, small stripper fewer, larger single-foot guides; big stripper ring
Handed-ness usually reel with the off hand same: cast right, crank left (most reels swap sides)

Guides and tiptop

Line comes off a spinning spool in big coils, so the first guide (the stripper) is large and sits high. The rest step down to choke the coils into a straight line. Use light single-foot guides to keep weight off the cane tip. A rule of thumb from the bamboorodmaking page is one guide per foot of rod, plus one.

Position (from tip) Ring size Notes
0" 6 mm ring, 6/64 tube across-corners at the tip ≈ 0.092", so 6/64 (0.094") fits
5" 6 mm
11" 6 mm
18" 7 mm
26" 8 mm
35" 10 mm just tip-side of the splice (36.75–41.25"), so it doubles as an alignment mark
47" 16 mm, high frame stripper, about 22" ahead of the reel foot; butt-side alignment mark

These are starting positions. Tape the guides on, mount the reel, and run the line through. Then do a static load test: tie the line off and bend the rod to about 90°, then move guides until the line follows the blank’s curve without touching it. Then cast with tape before wrapping. Wrap with fine thread, same as a fly rod; spinning guides don’t need special wrapping.

Reel

You want a 1000-size spinning reel (Shimano 1000 / Daiwa LT 1000–2000) that’s light (≈5.5–6.5 oz) and holds ~100+ yd of 4–6 lb mono. A heavier reel will make a 6'6" cane rod feel butt-heavy.

  • Modern pick: Shimano Stradic FM 1000HG (SKU ST1000HGFM): ~185 g / 6.5 oz, 6.0:1 gear, 3 kg drag. It’s the trout standard: smooth, durable, and easy to get serviced. FM is the current generation (the earlier one was FL), and HG means “high gear.”
  • Co-pick: Daiwa Ballistic MQ LT 1000: 6.2 oz on Field & Stream’s 2026 test scale. It’s the equal of the Stradic, so buy whichever is cheaper when you’re ready.
  • Shop by spec, not by name: 5.5–6.5 oz, 1000 size, aluminum spool, a drag that’s smooth at low settings (you’ll be running about 2 lb), and a handle that swaps sides. Published weights vary by source and model year, so confirm on the maker’s spec sheet. If you can, mount the reel on a rod in a shop to feel the balance.
  • Period-correct on cane: a vintage Mitchell 308 ultralight (the 408 is its faster-geared sibling: blue, with a screw-in handle). Check which side the handle cranks on any one you buy, because the vintage models vary. Look for a serviced one, because drags and bail springs on 50-year-old reels are the weak point.

Spinning basics for a fly angler:

  • Spool it right. Line comes off the filler spool the same direction it goes onto the reel, or you’ll fight twist all day. Fill to about 1/8" below the spool lip.
  • Set the drag to about 1/3 of the line test. With 6 lb line, the drag should slip at a ~2 lb pull on a scale.
  • Casting: pin the line on your index finger, open the bail, cast, and lift your finger to release. Touch the spool rim to feather or stop the lure. Close the bail by hand, not with the crank; that’s what stops line twist and loops.
  • Spinners twist line. Run a small ball-bearing swivel 18" ahead of any inline spinner.

Tackle

Everything below is single-hook or easy to convert, so the same box works on Hatchery Supported water (anything goes) and on the East Fork DH (one single hook, no bait). For DH, swap trebles for single siwash hooks with split rings and pliers, and take the second hook off a jerkbait.

Line: 6 lb mono for the mainstem; 4 lb is optional on the small DH runs. Mono is better than braid in December, because braid holds water and ices in the guides on freezing mornings. A 3’ 6 lb fluorocarbon leader is optional in gin-clear water.

Lure Size How to fish it in winter DH-legal?
Marabou or hair jig (black/olive, white) 1/32–1/16 oz Dead-drift or swim slowly along the bottom of deep pools. The top pick for cold water. ✅ single hook
Trout Magnet–style micro plastic on a 1/64 oz head 1/64 oz Under a small float through the slow pools. Deadly on stockers. ✅
2" curly-tail grub / small Ned rig 1/16 oz head Hop it slowly for winter smallmouth on the mainstem’s deep bends. ✅
Inline spinner (Panther Martin, Mepps #0–1, Rooster Tail) 1/16–1/8 oz Retrieve slowly, just fast enough to turn the blade. Swap to a single hook for DH. 🔧 convert
Spoon (Kastmaster, Phoebe) 1/12–1/8 oz Count it down, then flutter it back slowly. Good for long casts across the mainstem. 🔧 convert
Small floating or suspending minnow (Rapala F3/F5, CD3) ~1/8 oz Twitch and pause. Big browns and smallmouth will hit it. 🔧 one single hook
Nightcrawler on #8 hook + split shot — Hatchery Supported water only (bait banned on DH) ❌

Terminal kit: small ball-bearing swivels, round split shot (BB–#4), 1/2" float, #8 and #10 single hooks, single siwash hooks for conversions, a split-ring tool, forceps, a rubber-mesh net, and a small Plano box.

How to fish it: fish 11 a.m.–3 p.m., when the water is warmest. Fish slow and deep, close to the bottom of the deepest slow pools and the outside bends. Do several casts per spot before moving. Browns are spawning or just finished, so stay off redds: the clean, light-colored gravel patches.

Build checklist

  1. Check the taper: done in caneDNA (variant D, see Taper).
  2. Split culms into 5–6’ sections as in the class build. Stagger nodes 3×3, and keep them out of the 36–42" splice zone.
  3. Rough → heat-treat → finish each section on the standard bed. Mill the tip to 44" and the butt from 34" so both joints stay possible.
  4. Dry bind, then glue both sections.
  5. Choose the joint: cut and whip the 4.5" scarf bevels (36.75–41.25"), or trim square at 39" and fit a 12/64 ferrule.
  6. Shape the 12" cork; fit the reel foot and rings at about 8.5" from the butt.
  7. Tape the guides and do the static load test, then a casting test. Then wrap and finish.
  8. Buy the reel and line, then build the tackle box above.
  9. Before the first trip, confirm the Hap Simpson reach’s designation, the NCWRC stocking schedule, and USGS flows.

Graphite alternative: a Mud Hole build

This is the same rod in graphite, built from Mud Hole parts: a weekend build that fishes this winter while the cane rod is still in the binder. Everything else on this page (reel, line, tackle, how to fish it) carries over unchanged.

Blank: MHX S782-2

Tip size / butt 4.5 / 0.33" (8.50 mm) 4.5 / 0.33" (8.40 mm) 5.0 / 0.34"
Weight 1.25 oz 1.25 oz 1.4 oz
Price (Oct 2026) $61.00 $58.50 $66.25

The S782-2 matches the cane rod’s spec (6'6", light, 1/16-oz lures at the bottom of its range) and breaks down to about 40" for the car. Pick the S782 if you want the one-piece feel; the specs are identical. Pick the S842-2 if you want 6" more reach across the mainstem pools.

Handle: Fuji VSS split grip

This is Option B from Handle and reel seat, with real parts. The handle runs about 16" from the butt cap to the winding check:

  • Reel seat: Fuji VSS size 16 (VSSM-16). It’s 120 mm long with a 13.0 mm ID, the light size that suits a 1000 reel. The blank is 7.6–7.8 mm under the seat, so you’ll build up ~2.6 mm per side with an arbor (polyurethane arbor or masking-tape rings, epoxied).
  • Foregrip: Fuji contoured split grip, size 16, cork (FGVSS-16C, 3.75"). It’s made to mate with the VSS 16 nose.
  • Rear grip: American Tackle straight rear spinning grip, cork, 7", 0.250" ID (RG-7S-250), with a CBC-3 composite butt cap per the grip’s size chart. Ream the 0.250" bore out to the blank’s 8.0–8.5 mm. Dry-fit the tenon into the VSS’s rear nut before gluing, because Mud Hole doesn’t list this grip as a VSS match.
  • Winding check for a ~7.3 mm (0.29") blank at the front of the foregrip.

Guides: Fuji KL-H 169H kit (KR-style)

Mud Hole’s Fuji KL-H 169H kit is Fuji’s small-reel spinning train (“spinning up to 7'6"”), with Alconite rings on stainless frames. It’s a modern KR-style train: a small, high stripper close to the reel and an early choke guide that straightens the line, followed by a row of small identical runners. That’s lighter and casts farther than the old big-stripper layout. The 4.5 runners match the blank’s 4.5 tip.

Starting layout (inches from the tiptop; reel-foot center ≈ 68" from the tip):

# Guide Ring From tip Gap to next (toward butt)
tip Fuji LG micro spinning top, Alconite 4.5 ring / 4.5 tube 0 3.5"
1 KT runner 4.5 3.5" 4.0"
2 KT runner 4.5 7.5" 4.5"
3 KT runner 4.5 12" 5.0"
4 KT runner 4.5 17" 5.5"
5 KT runner 4.5 22.5" 6.0"
6 KB (transition) 4.5 28.5" 6.5"
7 KL 5.5M (choke) 5.5 35" 6.5"
8 KL 8H (reduction) 8 41.5" 6.5"
9 KL 16H (stripper) 16 48" ~20" to the reel foot

This is a starting point, not Fuji’s computed layout. Fuji’s 2009 “New Concept” chart for a 6'6" spinning rod puts a bigger stripper at about 45" from the tip with seven guides. This KR kit uses a smaller stripper and nine guides, so the spacing above is my adaptation. Before wrapping:

  1. Tape everything on.
  2. Run Fuji’s KR guide placement software (linked from Mud Hole’s KL and KT pages) with a 1000 reel and 6 lb mono.
  3. Do a static load test (bend to ~90°, line shouldn’t touch the blank).
  4. Do a cast test, watching the line cone: it should be choked to straight by guide 7.

On the S782-2, keep guide 8 off the ferrule. Mud Hole doesn’t publish the ferrule location. If a guide lands within ~1" of the female ferrule, slide it.

Bill of materials

Prices are Mud Hole’s listed prices as of Oct 31, 2026. A “verify” note means I couldn’t confirm that size’s SKU or price on the page.

Qty Item Mud Hole SKU Price Notes
1 MHX S782-2 6'6" Light Fast 2-pc blank, Slate S782-2-MHX $61.00 or S782-MHX 1-pc $58.50
1 Fuji VSS Standard spinning seat, size 16, BC Grey VSSM-16BC $5.77 120 mm, ID 13.0 mm; CC Silver also offered
1 Fuji contoured split foregrip, size 16, cork FGVSS-16C $9.39 3.75"
1 American Tackle straight rear spinning grip, cork, 7", 0.250" ID RG-7S-250 ~$8–12 (verify) the 4" is $8.19; ream to fit
1 American Tackle composite cork butt cap CBC-3 from $2.09 size per the rear-grip chart
1 Reel-seat arbor (polyurethane), or masking tape verify from $2.29 build ~7.7 → 13.0 mm
1 Winding check, ~7.3 mm (0.29") verify ~$1–3 Mud Hole trim parts
1 Fuji KL-H guide kit 169H, Alconite, BC Grey BCKLAG169H $28.90 KL16H, KL8H, KL5.5M, KB4.5, 5× KT4.5
1 Fuji LG micro spinning tip-top, Alconite, BC Grey, 4.5 ring / 4.5 tube verify size from $4.25 the tube must fit the 4.5 tip
1 Rod-wrapping thread, size A nylon — on hand same as the fly rods
— Rod finish (2-part) + grip/seat epoxy — on hand
Parts total ≈ $125 plus shipping; reel and line not included

Graphite build order

  1. Measure the blank’s spine and mark it; the guides go on the spine’s compression side.
  2. Ream and dry-fit the rear grip, the VSS seat on its arbor, and the foregrip. Glue them butt-first, seat aligned with the guide side.
  3. Fit the tip-top. Tape all guides on per the starting layout.
  4. Mount the reel, then do the static load test and cast test. Adjust.
  5. Wrap, finish, and cure. A graphite blank needs no varnish, just the guide wraps.

Sources

  • BambooRodmaking: spinning rod tapers: Tyree, T&T, P.H. Young, Bernard Hills, Montague-derived tapers, guide spacing
  • BambooRodmaking: one-piece rods: converting 2-piece tapers to one piece
  • Hexrod technical documentation
  • French Broad Paddle Trail access points
  • Swim Guide: French Broad at Hap Simpson Park: park facilities
  • Fly Fishing NC: Transylvania County trout streams: mainstem Hatchery Supported reach (third-party; verify)
  • NCWRC Delayed Harvest stocking schedule
  • NCWRC 2025 DH season press release: single-hook artificial rule
  • USGS 03443000 French Broad River at Blantyre
  • Field & Stream: best trout spinning reels (2026): Ballistic MQ LT 1000 tested weight
  • TackleDirect: Stradic FM ST1000HGFM: Stradic specs
  • Mud Hole product pages (Oct 31, 2026): MHX light spinning blanks, Fuji VSS seat, Fuji VSS foregrip, American Tackle rear grips, butt caps, Fuji KL-H guide kits, Fuji LG Alconite tip-top
  • MHX blank dimensions sheet (PDF)
  • Fuji, Spinning Rods: New Concept Guide Placement chart (via Mud Hole’s Fuji Concept Guide Spacing PDF)

item.title: Machining a Spinning Reel Seat and Building a Grip
item.description:
A plan and procedure for making the handle hardware of Rod 002, the 6'6" French Broad spinning rod myself: a machined reel seat (fixed hood plus a sliding threaded ring) and a cork grip built around it. The build log already covers two handle options: cork with two sliding rings (Option A) and a Fuji VSS skeleton seat on an arbor (Option B). This page is a third option: turn the seat from bar stock instead of buying it.

Status: plan only. Nothing here has been cut yet. The cane for Rod 002 hasn’t been milled either. Anything I haven’t measured or confirmed is marked to confirm, and every dimension below is a starting point, not a result.

What the repo does and doesn’t confirm

Item Status
Rod: 6'6", 2 pc, hex, light / moderate-fast, 1000-size reel Confirmed (build log)
Blank under the grip: 0.279–0.281″ (7.09–7.14 mm) Confirmed (build log spec table, taper table)
Reel-foot center about 8.5″ from the butt; 12″ cork handle in Option A Confirmed as Option A’s design value; still to be fine-tuned by balance
Fuji VSS 16 seat: 120 mm long, 13.0 mm ID (the graphite-blank option) Confirmed (build log, and re-checked on Mud Hole’s VSS page)
A cork-ring press exists as a printable tool Confirmed (printable rod tools)
Owning a metal lathe or mill Not stated anywhere in the repo (equipment.md is a stub; no page mentions a lathe). To confirm.
The reel’s foot dimensions To confirm. Measure the actual reel.
Thread size for the seat My choice, not a standard. See Threads.

If I don’t have a lathe, the fallback is Option A or B from the build log. Those need no machining. A wood lathe (or a drill with a support stand) is enough for the grip alone.

Choosing the style

Style How it holds the reel Pros Cons Fit for Rod 002
Sliding rings on cork (Option A in the log) Foot sits on bare cork, two rings slide over the ends Lightest; period-correct; no hardware Rings can creep when wet and cold Recommended in the log
Fixed hood + threaded ring (this page) Foot sits in a fixed hood; a threaded ring winds up against the other foot Locks solid; no creep; adjustable to the reel Needs machining and exact thread fit The one planned here
Hood and cap, no thread (slip-on sliding band) Same as the sliding rings but with metal-to-metal hoods Simple to make Same creep problem as rings Skip
Bought skeleton seat (Fuji VSS 16, Option B) Fixed hood plus a threaded hood and lock nut Cheap, tested, ~$6 Looks modern on cane; needs an arbor Fallback

A screw-lock seat (what the machined design is) beats a sliding band on a spinning rod because the reel foot takes the full pull of a hooked fish and the casting hand squeezes the seat. The band-only style is fine for light fly-style reels but is the one more likely to loosen.

Spinning-specific geometry

  • The reel hangs below the seat. The foot channel is open on the underside. The seat is a tube with a flat-bottomed (or slightly dished) cradle where the foot sits, a fixed hood at one end, and a threaded ring at the other that pulls the second foot tight.
  • Seat body OD: 7/8″ to 1″ (22–25 mm) is the usual range for finished spinning seats and the size my hand is likely to want on a light rod. Finished seat sizes vary by maker, so I’ll settle on a diameter from the reel and my grip (to confirm).
  • Reel foot gap. The distance between the fixed hood and the threaded ring at full open must exceed the foot-to-foot length of the reel, and at full closed must be less than the foot length. I’ll measure the 1000-size reel I’m going to use with calipers (to confirm) and make the channel about 1/4″ longer than that with the threaded ring’s travel at least that much.
  • Hex under a round bore. The butt is 0.279–0.281″ across flats, so the corners are 0.281 / cos 30° = 0.325″ (8.24 mm). A round bore smaller than that cuts into the corners. Mill the bore to clear the corners, or ream the bushing bore to the corner diameter and fill the gap (see Bushings).

Materials

Material Pros Cons Notes
6061-T6 aluminum Easy to turn; light; anodizes well; good thread life Needs finishing to look right; will gall on its own threads if both parts are bare My default pick
Brass (360 free-machining) Cuts beautifully; classic look on cane; heavy Heavier on a light rod; tarnishes unless lacquered Good for the threaded ring only
Stabilized or dense wood body with brass hardware Warm look; light Wood threads wear; moisture movement Use only for the body, with a metal insert for the threads
Nickel-silver The traditional bamboo-rod hardware Costly; harder to find in bar Not planned

Mixing the two (aluminum body, brass ring) avoids galling, because like metals tend to seize on fine threads. Anodize or lacquer the finished parts; see Finishing.

Measurements

All values are design targets, to confirm against the reel, the blank, and a test-fit.

Feature Target Notes
Blank under the seat 0.279–0.281″ across flats; 0.325″ across corners From the build log; measure the real cane
Bore of the seat body blank corners + clearance: 0.340–0.350″ Or bore to a bushing’s OD
Bushing OD / ID OD matches the seat bore; ID matches the tapered cane Cut from stock or build up from tape and epoxy
Seat body OD 0.875–1.000″ (22–25 mm) Pick from the reel and grip
Wall thickness ≥ 0.20″ at the thread root Check after the thread is cut
Thread 1″-20 UNEF, as a design choice (see below) Not a published reel-seat standard
Thread length on the body about 0.75″ 12–15 turns at 20 tpi
Reel foot channel foot length + about 0.25″ Measure the reel
Fixed hood height about 0.12–0.15″ above the foot bed To confirm against the foot
Reel-foot center from butt about 8.5″ From Option A in the log; adjust by balance
Total seat length about 4.0″ Hood + channel + ring travel
Fit tolerances thread: class 2A/2B; bore: ±0.002″ Reasonable shop targets

Threads

I didn’t find a published thread standard for spinning reel seat nuts. Manufacturers’ product pages (the Mud Hole pages I read) list length, ID, and OD but not the thread pitch, and different makers use different threads. So a machined seat can’t borrow a standard; I choose my own and both mating parts are mine.

  • Pick a common machinist thread so the tooling is on hand: 1″-20 UNEF (1″ major diameter, 20 tpi) is a good candidate for a ~1″ body. The thread depth is about 0.0325″, so the wall stays healthy. To confirm against the taps, dies, and single-point inserts I actually own.
  • Cut the male thread on the lathe (single-point, with the lathe geared for 20 tpi) rather than with a die. A die on 1″ aluminum cuts a rough thread and leaves it off-center. Take light passes and use cutting fluid.
  • Cut the ring’s female thread on the lathe too (boring bar or internal threading insert), then fit it to the body by sneaking up on the thread: stop when it runs freely with no radial shake.
  • Add relief at the end of the thread, so the ring can run up against the shoulder without bottoming on a half-cut thread.
  • Lock it: a thin nylon washer or a small O-ring under the ring’s face, or a second lock ring, so it doesn’t back off. To confirm which works.

Machining sequence

This is general machinist practice. I haven’t followed an opened reference for it (see Sources), so treat it as a plan to be checked on scrap first.

Lathe

  1. Cut bar stock (6061, about 1.25″ diameter, 5″ long) with about 1/2″ extra.
  2. Chuck it, face the end, and drill and bore through to the bore diameter. Bore first so the bore and the outside are concentric.
  3. Put the body on a mandrel (or chuck on the bore) and turn the outside to OD, leaving a shoulder for the fixed hood.
  4. Turn the thread relief, then single-point the male thread.
  5. Part off. Flip, face to length.
  6. Turn the threaded ring: bore, internal thread, then knurl or a hex OD if I want grip.
  7. Test-fit the ring on the body. Fit it before any other cuts.

Mill (if available)

  1. Cut the foot channel: a flat-bottomed slot across the bed width, with a ball-end or corner radius to match the foot.
  2. Open the underside window so the reel foot can sit on the cane or bushing side.
  3. Drill any vent or pin holes (a small hole to relieve epoxy, and any set-screw I want).

If I don’t have a mill: cut the channel on the lathe with a slotting setup, or file it by hand with a jig. To confirm.

Finishing

Option Pros Cons
Hard-coat or color anodize (aluminum) Tough; many colors Needs a vendor or a home kit; coat is thick, so the threads must be cut oversize/undersize to allow for it (to confirm with the anodizer)
Bead-blast, then clear lacquer Easy; matte look Wears at the thread
Polish (brass) Classic on cane Tarnishes; needs lacquer or regular wax
Leave bare, clear-coat only on non-thread surfaces Works Needs periodic cleaning

Anodizing adds a few ten-thousandths per surface, so cut the threads and fit them before anodizing, then re-check the fit. Masking the threads during anodizing is the usual alternative.

Bushings and bonding to the blank

  1. Fit the seat to the cane first, dry. Slide the seat over the butt. It should go on freely at the corners with no rocking.
  2. Make bushings (two, one at each end of the seat): aluminum or brass rings, or turned from epoxy-filled phenolic, with a bore that matches the cane’s taper at that point and an OD that matches the seat bore. Where the bore is round and the blank is hex, either fill the gaps with thickened epoxy or turn tape-and-epoxy bushings in place.
  3. Mask the cane above and below the bonding area, and the seat’s threads and channel, with painter’s tape.
  4. Epoxy with a slow-cure (30-minute or longer) 2-part epoxy. equipment.md records a recommendation of 3M DP2216 for ferrule glue; I could use the same adhesive here (to confirm it suits an aluminum-to-cane bond; the repo only recommends it for ferrules). Use a thin film, and keep it off the threads.
  5. Align the seat so the reel hangs on the same side as the guides, then hold it square with the blank for the cure. A tape alignment mark on the butt helps.
  6. Wipe squeeze-out with denatured alcohol before it gels.

The grip

Cork rings vs. shaped cork

Option Pros Cons
Cork rings, glued up and turned Cheap; pick the best rings for the high-touch spots; any shape Takes time; voids need filling
Pre-shaped cork grip (the Option B parts in the log: Fuji split fore/rear grips) Ready to ream and glue Limited shapes; sized for a particular seat

I’m using rings here since the machined seat doesn’t match a commercial grip.

Ring dimensions and count

  • Standard ring: 1 1/4″ OD, 1/2″ thick, 1/4″ bore. That’s the size Mud Hole’s overstock cork rings list (page opened). Sizes and grades vary by maker; the “grade” label is a seller’s, not a standard.
  • Rear grip: 7″ is the build log’s choice for the Option B rear grip, about 14 rings at 1/2″. To confirm for this rod (the handle is 12″ total in Option A).
  • Foregrip: about 3.75″ (as in the log), about 7-8 rings.
  • A 1 1/4″ ring leaves about 0.125–0.25″ for shaping around a 1″ seat, so grips that are bigger than the seat are possible but not by much. Larger rings exist; to confirm stock.
  • Buy a few extras and hand-pick: put the best rings where the thumb and palm sit, and the worst at the ends where washers dent them.

Glue-up

  1. Bore each ring to just under the blank (a tapered rattail file or reamer on a drill) and put them on a waxed mandrel or threaded rod. Rings arrive with a 1/4″ bore; the cane is 0.28–0.33″ at the grip, so ring bores should be opened slightly.
  2. Glue sparingly. Enough that the inner surface just shines; excess glue forces epoxy onto the mandrel and the grip’s outside, and the grip can become nearly impossible to remove.
  3. Press the stack: washers and nuts on threaded rod, or the printable cork press from this site. Tighten until glue just oozes between the rings.
  4. Put a low-grade ring at each end to absorb the press marks.
  5. Cure fully, overnight and a bit more. Reaming too soon makes the grip come apart.

Turning and shaping

  • On a lathe or a drill with a support stand: true the stack to a cylinder with 60-grit on a flat board, then rough the profile, leaving a little extra, then work up through the grits. One builder ends at 320 grit.
  • Shaping without a lathe: fold sandpaper into a firm corner and work wells into the spinning grip; a rasp for the first roughing.
  • Calipers at the high points; stop slightly above the final diameter.
  • Dust: cork dust is fine and gets everywhere. Work outdoors or with a shop vacuum at the grip.

Fitting and fill

  • Remove the grip from the mandrel by gripping it with both hands and striking the mandrel on a flat, solid surface.
  • Ream to the blank and test-fit, then bond with epoxy, as with the seat. Put the rear grip on first against the seat’s rear edge and the foregrip against the fixed hood.
  • Fill voids after shaping and before the final sanding: a cork dust and epoxy (or wood-filler) paste, pushed in, left proud, sanded flush.
  • Burnish with a hard smooth surface or a very fine paper (400-grit or finer) to close the surface. (General practice, not from a cited source.)
  • Winding check (in the log’s Option B notes: for a roughly 7.3 mm blank): fit at the front of the foregrip, then wrap and finish.
  • Finish: leave the cork bare or seal it lightly, per taste. To confirm.

Parts and materials

Qty Item Notes
1 6061-T6 aluminum round bar, about 1.25″ x 5″ For the body
1 Brass bar (360), about 1.25″ x 2″ For the threaded ring, optional
2 Bushings (aluminum, brass, or tape-and-epoxy) Sized to the cane at the seat
20–25 Cork rings, 1 1/4″ x 1/2″ x 1/4″ Spare rings for matching and for voids
1 Waxed mandrel or threaded rod, about 5/16″ Matches the bore after reaming
1 Rattail file or tapered reamer For opening the ring bores
— Sandpaper, 60 to 320 grit, and a flat board Hand shaping
— 2-part slow-cure epoxy Seat bonding and grip bonding
— Wood glue (Titebond II or similar) Ring-to-ring
— Painter’s tape, denatured alcohol, nylon washer or O-ring Masking, cleanup, ring lock
— Winding check Per the log
— Anodize or lacquer Finish

Tools: lathe with single-point threading and a boring bar (to confirm I have this), calipers, a thread gauge, optionally a mill, the printed cork press.

Troubleshooting

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Ring binds or won’t start on the body Thread over-cut, or chips in the thread, or the anodize added thickness Clean; re-chase; ease the thread after anodizing
Ring loosens when wet No lock; thread too coarse for the load Add an O-ring or nylon washer; add a lock ring
Seat wobbles on the blank Bushings oversize or too thin Re-fit; thicken the epoxy; recheck alignment while curing
Seat won’t slide on over the hex corners Bore smaller than 0.325″ across corners Bore to 0.340″+ or use bushings
Grip glue line shows Too much glue between the rings Use less; sand back a little
Grip cracks on reaming Reamed before cure; too fast Wait; ream in steps
Voids in the finished cork Poor rings Fill and sand; move low-grade rings to the ends
Reel rattles in the seat Channel too long or the hood too shallow Shim with tape, or recut with a tighter channel
Cork dust everywhere Dry sanding Outdoors or with a vacuum

Safety

  • Lathe PPE: safety glasses or face shield; no loose sleeves, gloves, or jewelry; long hair tied back; chuck key out before power on. Run the lathe at a sensible speed for the stock size, and stand out of the line of the chuck. Remove burrs and sharp edges before handling parts.
  • Threading: cut aluminum with light passes and coolant; watch for stringy chips and don’t clear them by hand.
  • Cork dust: wear a dust mask (N95 or better) and use dust collection; work outdoors or with a shop vacuum.
  • Epoxy: nitrile gloves and ventilation; solvents (alcohol) away from ignition sources; don’t use epoxy past its working time.
  • Anodizing chemicals (if home-done): acids, gloves, goggles, and disposal rules. To confirm whether I’d do that or send it out.

Sources

I opened and read these for this page. They cover the grip and the seat sizing; I did not find an opened source for reel-seat thread specs or for turning a reel seat from bar stock, so those sections are my own plan.

  • Global FlyFisher: Making Grips II (archive): off-blank ring glue-up, mandrel sizing, Titebond, 60-grit to 320-grit turning, ring prices
  • In-Fisherman: 7 Reminders for Building Custom Cork Grips (archive): waxing the mandrel, sparing glue, composite vs. standard cork, removing the grip
  • Mud Hole: 4 Steps to Shape Custom Cork Grips (archive): spinning-mandrel shaping, reaming, bonding with epoxy
  • Mud Hole product pages, for dimensions: Fuji VSS Standard seat (archive), overstock cork rings (archive)

Back to the Rod 002 build log.

item.title: 3D-Printed Rodmaking Tools
item.description:
Small shop tools for the bamboo build process. The blank-making tools tie to steps of the Morgan Hand Mill workflow; the grip, ferrule, and finishing tools serve the later stages the class notes stop short of. All are FDM-printable in PETG or PLA, generated parametrically, and validated watertight. STLs export in print orientation.

Parametric source: generate_rod_tools_stls.py — edit the parameter block (indicator stem size, ferrule bore, PVC diameter) and re-run to fit your hardware.

Depth-gauge base

For: checking strip dimensions over steel planing forms — the “set taper from spreadsheet” and final-planing steps.

A 70 × 40 base that rides the flats of the planing form on two end pads (the middle is relieved so bamboo dust doesn’t tilt it). A 3/8"-stem dial indicator drops through the centre bore and a printed pinch slit with an M4 cross-bolt clamps it: the socket-head bolt drives through a deep access tunnel on one side, and the nut drops into a top-loaded hex track on the other. Fit a 60° contact point to the indicator and it reads strip depth in the form groove directly.

depth_gauge_base.stl · print 1 · hardware: M4 × 35 socket-head bolt + nut, dial indicator with 3/8" stem and 60° point

Node-sanding jig

For: “sand nodes on disc sander until flat & flush with enamel” — the fancy sanding jig the class notes tell you to use if you have one.

A 90 mm block with an 8.2 mm channel: the strip lies enamel-down with the node proud of the face, and the printed tapered wedge presses in alongside to friction-lock it — no hardware at all. Present the jig face to the disc sander and the node sands dead flush without dishing the strip on either side.

node_sanding_jig.stl + node_jig_wedge.stl · print 1 each · no hardware

Strip-sanding plate

For: flattening/leveling the enamel face along a strip’s full length — the hand-sanding counterpart to the node jig above.

A 250 mm plate with a 60° V-channel down its length. The strip drops in point-down on its beveled (pith-side) edge; the enamel face sits proud above the flat rails on either side. Run a flat sanding board over the top — once the board rides the rails flush, the enamel face is level for the whole length, and the rails stop you from sanding past it.

strip_sanding_plate.stl · print 1 · no hardware

Binding-cord spool caddy

For: cord payoff during binding — implements the Garrison article’s spool fix.

The bulk cord spool rides an M8 axle that drops into open cradle slots in the two uprights. The Ø3.5 socket in the base takes a 1/8" brass rod bent into an overhead loop: cord comes off the spool up through the loop, and the springy rod absorbs tension spikes instead of passing them into the wrap — the exact shock-absorber trick from the Garrison Binder article.

spool_caddy.stl · print 1 · hardware: M8 × 120 bolt (or M8 rod) + washers, ~300 mm of 1/8" brass rod, 4 wood screws

Cork press

For: gluing up a grip from cork rings.

Two Ø60 pressure discs and two six-lobed knobs with captive M8 nuts. Stack glued cork rings on a length of M8 threaded rod between the discs, spin the knobs down, and leave it to cure. Press the grip off-rod, then ream to the blank and glue it on.

cork_press_disc.stl ×2 · cork_press_knob.stl ×2 · hardware: M8 threaded rod ~300 mm

Finishing V-stands

For: supporting and hand-turning a blank during wrap finishing and varnish work.

120 mm-tall stands with a deep 90° V. Glue felt into the V so the blank turns without marking. Print two (or three for long butt sections) and screw them to a board at whatever spacing the section needs.

finishing_v_stand.stl ×2 · hardware: felt strip, 4 wood screws

Ferrule slitting collar

For: cutting even serrations in ferrule tangs.

A collar that slips over the ferrule with six 0.7 mm saw-guide slots. The slots stop 4 mm above the base, so the jeweler’s saw bottoms out at a consistent depth and the cuts land at exactly 60° spacing. The bore is parametric — regenerate for each ferrule size you use (the included STL is Ø7.0).

ferrule_slit_collar.stl · print per ferrule size · hardware: jeweler’s saw

Varnish dip-tube cap

For: dust-free drying after dip-varnishing in a 1.5" PVC tube.

Caps the tube; the Ø10 centre hole passes the hanging wire so the freshly dipped section can drip and dry inside, sealed from shop dust. It prints pocket-up with zero overhang — flip it over to fit the tube. Regenerate PVC_OD if your tube measures differently.

dip_cap.stl · print 1

Print settings

PETG or PLA, 0.2 mm layers, 3–4 perimeters, 30–40% infill. No supports on any part. The depth-gauge base benefits from a dead-flat first layer — print it alone on a clean bed.

Related

  • Morgan Hand Mill — the build process these tools serve
  • 3D-Printed Garrison Binder — the binder these support
  • Ring-Flyer Orbit Binder — design study for an orbiting-spool binder

item.title: Miscellaneous
item.description:
Chopsticks, Why Not

I’m going to have a load of extra bamboo strips, so why not use them.

Peak Bamboo

Peak Bamboo (Wayback Machine) has a PDF published about how to make bamboo chopsticks (Wayback Machine).

I’m going to give this a shape, marking out a taper and building it.
